title: SIEM-ready Audit Export (Beta) — Positioning notes for Splunk + Datadog
content:
Working doc for AEs/SEs/PMM: how to pitch SIEM-ready audit export (beta), handle common objections, and guide security reviewers toward the right proof points.

Last updated notes reflect current beta scope: sinks = Splunk HEC, Datadog Logs intake, S3 (incl SSE-KMS); delivery semantics = at-least-once; filtering supported; schema versioned (Audit Event v1). Feature is controlled via per-tenant feature flag.

---

1) What it is (one-liner + why it matters)

One-liner
- “Redwood can export audit events (admin + security-relevant actions) directly into your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog) or to S3, so your SOC can correlate Redwood activity with the rest of your environment.”

Why customers care
- Security teams don’t want “yet another console.” They want Redwood events where incident response already happens.
- Helps with SOC 2 / ISO evidence (who did what, when, from where) and internal monitoring.
- Reduces manual support escalations: customers can self-diagnose access/config changes via SIEM searches.

What it is not
- Not a “full data lake export” or application logs export. This is audit events (control-plane + security/admin actions), not request/response payload logging.
- Not exactly-once delivery. It’s at-least-once; duplicates are possible. We provide dedupe keys and guidance.
- Beta is not “every SIEM vendor under the sun.” Splunk, Datadog, S3 only.

---

2) Primary positioning pillars

Pillar A: Production-grade delivery guarantees (reliability first)
- At-least-once delivery with durable buffering + retries/backoff + explicit failure states.
- Per-destination health status surfaced in Console (and via API) so customers can detect degraded exports.
- Replay tooling for a time window (operator/customer workflow depending on deployment + support plan).

Pillar B: Noise/cost controls (filtering)
- Customer-configurable filters so only relevant audit signals flow into SIEM (reduce ingest cost, reduce alert fatigue).
- Filters can include/exclude by event type, actor, workspace/tenant, environment, and time window; optional IP/region constraints when available.

Pillar C: SIEM-ready schema (stable + versioned)
- Published schema v1 with consistent fields for correlation: event_id, event_time, actor, target, workspace/tenant ids, environment, request_id/correlation ids, source IP (when available), user agent (when available), result/outcome.
- Schema evolution rules: versioned; additive changes preferred; deprecations communicated.

Pillar D: Works across deployment modes
- Hosted, Dedicated, and Private supported (beta scope: “supported” means we have an operable pathway; Private may require deployment coordination / egress allowlisting).

Pillar E: Security posture built in
- Credentials stored encrypted; least-privilege guidance for S3 IAM/KMS policies.
- RBAC gates for who can configure exports; export config changes themselves are audited.
- Destination misconfiguration risk acknowledged with validations + “test delivery” UX.

---

3) How to talk about Splunk vs Datadog vs S3 (choose the right narrative)

Splunk HEC narrative (security / SOC teams)
- Best for orgs with Splunk as the “source of truth” for security alerts + compliance searches.
- Highlight: HEC batching + optional ACK mode for stronger delivery confidence.
- “Works with your existing Splunk parsing & dashboards; we emit consistent fields designed for correlation.”

Datadog Logs narrative (platform + DevSecOps teams)
- Best for customers already using Datadog for logs/metrics/traces and wanting a single observability surface.
- Highlight: regional intake endpoints; tagging guidance; log pipeline parsing recommendations.

S3 narrative (regulated / backfill / long retention)
- Best for customers that want ownership of raw event storage, long retention, or “bring-your-own SIEM” downstream.
- Highlight: partitioning by tenant/date/hour, gzip compression, SSE-KMS; compatible with data lake ingestion patterns.
- Positioning: “S3 gives you maximum control; Splunk/Datadog gives you fastest time-to-detection.”

---

4) Talk tracks (by persona)

CISO / Security Lead
- “We export audit events into Splunk/Datadog/S3 so your SOC can detect and investigate changes to access, keys, and policy—without relying on manual console review.”
- “The exporter is designed for reliability (durable buffering, retries, health visibility) and a stable schema suitable for correlation.”

Security Engineer / SOC Analyst
- “Events include actor + action + target + outcome + correlation identifiers. You can build detections like: unusual admin actions, key rotations, RBAC changes, and export config changes.”
- “We provide dedupe keys and recommend idempotent indexing; duplicates are expected under at-least-once semantics.”

Platform Engineer
- “It’s configurable, filterable, and operable. You can pause a destination, see last success/error, and control export volume.”

GRC / Compliance
- “Audit export supports evidence needs by preserving an immutable trail in customer-controlled systems; export configuration is access-controlled and itself audited.”
- “Schema is versioned and documented; changes are communicated.”

---

5) Common objections + responses

Objection: “Do you guarantee exactly-once delivery?”
Response:
- “For the beta we guarantee at-least-once delivery. That means duplicates are possible during retries/failover.”
- “We include a unique event_id plus stable dedupe guidance. Splunk/Datadog have patterns to dedupe or treat duplicates safely. For S3, we use idempotent naming/partitioning strategy guidance.”
- “We chose at-least-once because it’s the most reliable approach under real-world network failures and sink throttling; exactly-once is often illusory across third-party sinks.”

Objection: “If it’s at-least-once, can you at least preserve ordering?”
Response:
- “We do not promise global ordering. We preserve per-destination checkpointing and provide event_time and IDs so downstream queries can sort. Ordering guarantees across retries and partitions are not realistic at scale.”

Objection: “What’s the lag? We need near-real-time.”
Response:
- “We target low delivery latency, but it depends on sink throttling and filter volume. We have delivery latency SLOs and dashboards; if the sink is returning 429/5xx we back off and buffer rather than drop.”
- “We can set expectations during beta: typical seconds-to-minutes; worst-case bounded by backlog and sink health. We provide health indicators + backlog estimates.”

Objection: “Can I export historical events (backfill)?”
Response:
- “Full historical backfill for all tenants is out of scope for beta. We do support replaying a defined time window as an operational tool, with safeguards.”

Objection: “Will this leak sensitive data / prompts?”
Response:
- “Audit export is not request payload logging. The schema is explicitly designed to avoid prompt/content data. We follow PII redaction guidance for actor identifiers and include only what’s needed for security correlation.”

Objection: “How do you secure the destination credentials?”
Response:
- “Credentials are encrypted at rest and access-controlled. For S3 we recommend least-privilege IAM and SSE-KMS. For Splunk/Datadog keys/tokens, we provide rotation guidance and errors are classified clearly (auth vs throttling).”

Objection: “We’re Private/on-prem; we can’t allow broad egress.”
Response:
- “S3 (or S3-compatible storage) is typically the best fit for Private because it can be within the customer’s network boundary. For Splunk/Datadog, we’ll need explicit egress allowlisting and endpoint planning.”

Objection: “This is just table stakes; why not use cloud provider audit logs?”
Response:
- “Cloud provider logs don’t capture application-level Redwood actions (RBAC changes, API key rotations, workspace admin changes, export config changes). This fills the gap with a stable schema and SIEM-ready fields.”

---

6) Competitive comparisons (keep it factual)

Compared to “roll your own” (webhook + lambda)
- Pros of Redwood: reliable delivery primitives (durable queueing, retries/backoff, DLQ), filtering built-in, schema versioning, operability (health views + runbooks), and support.
- Acknowledge: If a customer only needs “dump everything somewhere,” a DIY webhook may be quicker but usually becomes brittle at scale.

Compared to general cloud AI platforms
- Cloud platforms may offer audit logs for their own consoles, but not a unified, developer-first schema tied to Redwood tenants/workspaces/environments across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.
- Redwood provides consistent event taxonomy even when deployment mode changes.

Compared to “LLM API providers”
- Many provide minimal audit trails or only basic admin events; Redwood’s bet is operability + schema stability + delivery reliability as a first-class product.

Compared to inference infrastructure vendors (self-host runtimes)
- Those products may not provide an out-of-the-box control plane export with enterprise-grade operational tooling; Redwood does and supports multiple sinks.

Language to avoid
- Don’t claim “exactly-once,” “zero loss,” or “guaranteed real-time.” Use “at-least-once,” “durable buffering,” “observable health,” and “configurable filters.”

---

7) Proof points to offer during security reviews (what to show / what to say)

Artifacts (internal links; customer-facing versions via docs)
- Audit Event Schema v1 (field definitions + examples)
- Delivery semantics ADR (at-least-once rationale, dedupe strategy)
- Sink ADRs (Splunk HEC auth/ACK model; S3 partitioning + SSE-KMS)
- SLOs page (delivery latency + success rate targets; hosted vs private differences)
- Setup guides: Splunk HEC + Datadog intake
- Terraform examples for S3 least-privilege policies and KMS key policy patterns

Operational proof points
- “We can show dashboard views of: delivery latency, success/failure rate by sink, backlog depth, DLQ volume, and top error classes.”
- “We have runbooks for backlog drain/replay and for credential rotation issues.”

Security controls proof points
- RBAC: who can create/update/pause destinations
- Audit trail for export configuration changes
- Encryption: SSE-KMS for S3; encrypted secret storage for tokens/keys

Beta-specific disclosure (say this early)
- “Beta feature: enabled by feature flag; sink support limited; some operational tooling continues to evolve (e.g., more granular error surfaces, expanded replay self-serve).”

---

8) Suggested customer-facing phrasing (copy/paste snippets)

Delivery guarantee snippet
- “Audit export is delivered with at-least-once semantics. In rare cases (e.g., retries after network/sink errors), you may observe duplicate events. Each event includes a unique event_id you can use for deduplication.”

Filtering snippet
- “You can reduce SIEM ingest volume by filtering exports by event types, actors, workspaces/tenants, environments, and time windows.”

Security snippet
- “Destination credentials are stored encrypted and access-controlled. Export destination configuration changes are permissioned and recorded as audit events.”

---

9) Field guidance (what customers should key on)

Strong correlation fields
- event_id (dedupe)
- event_time (sorting)
- request_id / correlation_id (trace across systems)
- actor.id / actor.type (user vs service)
- workspace_id / tenant_id
- environment (prod/stage/etc)
- source.ip (when present)
- action/event_type (taxonomy)
- outcome/result (success/failure)

What to set expectations on
- IP/geo may be “unknown” for some internal-to-internal operations (depends on request path).
- Some events are high volume; recommend filters for “read-only” events if available (beta focus is on security/admin change events).

---

10) Open questions / follow-ups (for next revision)

- Confirm final beta taxonomy list for “security-critical” event types vs “operational noise.”
- Validate recommended Splunk sourcetype + CIM mapping suggestion (partner feedback pending).
- Decide how we talk about replay tooling availability (self-serve vs support-assisted) by deployment mode.
- Pricing/packaging: confirm whether SIEM export is in enterprise compliance bundle vs add-on before wide enablement.
